thing: Space Shuttle solid rocket booster field-joint O-ring seals
claim: Cold-weather O-ring blow-by in the booster field joints could cause loss of a shuttle and its crew.
what_happened: Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after a 28 Jan 1986 launch at record cold when a right SRB field-joint O-ring failed; Rogers Commission confirmed the cause.
dismissed_by: Morton Thiokol management and NASA Marshall managers, who reversed a no-launch recommendation the night before
cost_of_error: 7 astronauts killed, orbiter lost, shuttle fleet grounded 32 months
lesson: When the engineers closest to the data say no-go and management reverses them under schedule pressure, the burden of proof has been inverted and the warning is the signal.

quotes.text: The result would be a catastrophe of the highest order - loss of human life.
quotes.speaker: Roger Boisjoly (memo to Morton Thiokol VP Engineering)

thing: Space Shuttle Columbia (STS-107) after a launch foam strike on the left wing
claim: The foam strike may have caused serious wing damage, and NASA should obtain outside imagery of the orbiter before re-entry.
what_happened: Columbia disintegrated on re-entry on 1 Feb 2003 after hot gas entered a breach in the left-wing leading edge made by the foam strike; the CAIB confirmed the cause.
dismissed_by: Mission Management Team chair Linda Ham, who cancelled the DoD imagery request; foam strikes had been normalised as a maintenance issue
cost_of_error: 7 astronauts killed, orbiter lost, shuttle flights halted ~2.5 years, program retired 2011
lesson: A hazard that has happened many times without disaster gets reclassified as normal; treat repeated near-misses as data about the tail, not proof of safety.

quotes.text: Remember the NASA safety posters everywhere around stating, 'If it's not safe, say so'? Yes, it's that serious.
quotes.speaker: Rodney Rocha, NASA structural engineer (unsent email, quoted in CAIB report)
quotes.publication: Columbia Accident Investigation Board report ch.6, via Spaceflight Now

quotes.text: In my humble technical opinion, this is the wrong (and bordering on irresponsible) answer from the SSP and Orbiter not to request additional imaging help from any outside source.
quotes.speaker: Rodney Rocha, NASA structural engineer (unsent email, quoted in CAIB report)
quotes.publication: Columbia Accident Investigation Board report ch.6, via Spaceflight Now

thing: Boeing 737 MAX Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS)
claim: MCAS behaved erratically in simulation, could activate repeatedly off a single sensor, and pilots could take too long to recover from it.
what_happened: Lion Air 610 (Oct 2018) and Ethiopian 302 (Mar 2019) crashed after erroneous MCAS activation; the MAX was grounded worldwide for ~20 months and the House found Boeing withheld test data from the FAA.
dismissed_by: Boeing management and the FAA's delegated certification process; MCAS was kept out of pilot manuals to avoid simulator training
cost_of_error: 346 deaths; $2.5bn Justice Department settlement (2021); fleet grounded ~20 months
lesson: When competitive pressure makes a known flaw expensive to disclose, internal test data that never reaches the regulator is the warning, and delegated self-certification will not surface it.

quotes.text: I’m levelling off at like 4000 ft, 230 knots and the plane is trimming itself like crazy. I’m like, WHAT?
quotes.speaker: Mark Forkner, Boeing 737 MAX chief technical pilot (internal message, Nov 2016)

quotes.text: The MAX crashes were… a horrific culmination of a series of faulty technical assumptions by Boeing’s engineers, a lack of transparency on the part of Boeing’s management, and grossly insufficient oversight by the FAA
quotes.speaker: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure final report

claim: Hydrogen lift gas was too flammable for passenger airships; the Hindenburg was designed for non-flammable helium for that reason.
what_happened: R101 burned after crashing in France in 1930 and the hydrogen-filled Hindenburg burned at Lakehurst in May 1937, ending the rigid passenger airship era.
dismissed_by: Luftschiffbau Zeppelin, which flew on hydrogen after the US Helium Act of 1925 export ban held, betting on careful operations
cost_of_error: 36 dead at Lakehurst (1937); 48 dead on R101 (1930); commercial airship travel effectively ended
lesson: When the safe input is unavailable and you substitute the dangerous one while keeping the original business plan, you have accepted the risk the design was built to avoid.

thing: Tacoma Narrows suspension bridge with slender 8-ft plate-girder stiffening (Moisseiff design)
claim: The state's own engineer (Clark Eldridge) specified 25-ft-deep stiffening trusses; the slimmer, cheaper girder deck substituted for it lacked the stiffness the span needed.
what_happened: The bridge oscillated visibly from opening day (nicknamed Galloping Gertie) and tore itself apart in a 40 mph wind on 7 Nov 1940, four months after opening; aeroelastic flutter became a core design check.
dismissed_by: Federal funders (PWA/RFC) and consulting engineer Leon Moisseiff, whose cheaper deflection-theory design was preferred as more elegant and less costly
cost_of_error: An $8m bridge (approx. $183m today) destroyed four months after opening; no human deaths
lesson: A celebrated new theory that lets you build lighter and cheaper is exactly where an untested failure mode hides; the conservative design's extra cost was the price of the unknown.

thing: Combustible ACM cladding refurbishment on Grenfell Tower and the fire-safety regime around high-rise social housing
claim: Residents warned the landlord was ignoring fire safety at Grenfell and that only a catastrophic event would expose it; earlier cladding fires (Knowsley Heights 1991, Lakanal House 2009) had shown exterior panels spread fire.
what_happened: On 14 June 2017 a fridge fire spread up the newly clad 24-storey tower; the 2024 Inquiry found decades of regulatory, industry and landlord failure and deemed the deaths avoidable.
dismissed_by: Kensington and Chelsea TMO and council, which threatened the bloggers with legal action; government slow-walked post-Lakanal regulatory review
cost_of_error: 72 deaths, 74 injured; property loss est. £200m-£1bn; national cladding remediation programme costing billions
lesson: Warnings from the people living with a risk get dismissed as complaints rather than data; when they cite prior incidents of the same failure mode, treat them as the early-warning system.

quotes.text: only a catastrophic event will expose the ineptitude and incompetence of [KCTMO]
quotes.speaker: Grenfell Action Group blog (as quoted on Wikipedia)

thing: OceanGate Titan carbon-fibre-hull crewed submersible, uncertified, for Titanic-wreck tourism
claim: The uncertified carbon-fibre hull had not been non-destructively tested and the acoustic monitoring would warn only milliseconds before an implosion; the experimental approach could end catastrophically.
what_happened: Titan imploded on 18 June 2023 during a dive to the Titanic wreck, killing all five aboard including CEO Stockton Rush.
dismissed_by: CEO Stockton Rush, who fired and sued Lochridge and told the Marine Technology Society that industry standards were stifling innovation
cost_of_error: 5 deaths; multinational search costing millions; OceanGate ceased operations
lesson: When a founder frames certification as the enemy of innovation and answers a safety whistleblower with a lawsuit, the warning is no longer about engineering but about governance.

quotes.text: only show when a component is about to fail – often milliseconds before an implosion
quotes.speaker: David Lochridge, OceanGate director of marine operations (2018 report, as quoted on Wikipedia)

quotes.text: unanimous concern regarding the development of 'TITAN' and the planned Titanic Expedition
quotes.speaker: Marine Technology Society Submarine Group draft letter to Stockton Rush (as quoted on Wikipedia)

thing: Ford Pinto subcompact with rear-mounted fuel tank
claim: The Pinto's fuel tank placement made it a firetrap in low-speed rear-end collisions, and Ford knowingly skipped a cheap fix on cost-benefit grounds.
what_happened: NHTSA found a defect and Ford recalled 1.5 million Pintos and Bobcats in 1978; Grimshaw jury awarded $125m punitive damages. Later analyses (Schwartz 1991; Lee & Ermann 1999) found the Pinto's overall fire-fatality rate roughly average for its class and the death tolls claimed in Pinto Madness unsupported.
dismissed_by: Ford, whose recall evaluation group twice found no actionable issue and which lobbied NHTSA against tougher fuel-system rules with a cost-benefit memo
cost_of_error: 1.5m-car recall (1978); Grimshaw award $127.8m by jury, cut to $3.5m punitive; Indiana criminal homicide prosecution (Ford acquitted 1980); lasting reputational damage
lesson: A real, narrow defect can be right while the headline casualty count is wrong; the durable damage came from a cost-benefit memo that read as pricing lives, not from the fire statistics.

thing: Takata airbag inflators using phase-stabilized ammonium nitrate propellant
claim: Ammonium nitrate propellant was unstable and prone to uncontrolled explosion, so inflators could rupture and spray metal fragments at occupants.
what_happened: Inflators degraded in heat and humidity and ruptured; NHTSA ordered a 42m+ vehicle US recall (largest in US history), over 100m inflators recalled worldwide, Takata pleaded guilty to fraud and went bankrupt in 2017.
dismissed_by: Takata management, which chose the cheaper propellant over engineers' objections and later manipulated test data
cost_of_error: At least 16 deaths per DOJ at plea (later counts 20+ worldwide), hundreds injured; $1bn guilty-plea settlement; company bankrupt and sold for ~$1.6bn
lesson: A cheaper input chosen over engineers' stability objections can sit dormant for a decade and then fail at fleet scale, so the time between warning and harm says nothing about whether the warning was wrong.

quotes.text: At the meeting, I literally said that if we go forward with this, somebody will be killed.
quotes.speaker: Mark Lillie, former Takata propellant engineer (to Bloomberg, as quoted)
quotes.publication: Newsome Melton blog quoting Bloomberg and Japan Times

claim: Supersonic airliners would never pay: fuel burn, sonic-boom overland bans and noise would cap demand far below forecasts.
what_happened: The US cancelled its SST in 1971 after spending over $1bn; Concorde's forecast of 350 sales collapsed to 20 built, with only the state-backed Air France and British Airways taking delivery, and the fleet retired in 2003.
dismissed_by: British and French governments and the BAC/Sud consortium, bound by a treaty with heavy cancellation penalties and national prestige
cost_of_error: Development costs ran more than six times projections; unit cost £23m in 1977; only 20 aircraft built versus 350 forecast and 100+ options; development never recouped (BA later ran it at an operating profit after the capital was written off)
lesson: Non-binding options and national prestige are not demand; if the product's physics bars it from most of the market (overland routes), the forecast is fiction no matter how impressive the engineering.

quotes.text: one of aerospace's most ambitious but commercially flawed projects
quotes.speaker: Flight International (as quoted on Wikipedia)

thing: Hyperloop low-pressure tube pod transport (Musk Alpha white paper, Hyperloop One and others)
claim: The $6bn LA-SF cost estimate and cheap fares were wildly understated; tube alignment, power, safety and low capacity would keep the economics from ever working.
what_happened: A decade on, no passenger hyperloop was built; Hyperloop One dropped passengers in 2022 and shut down on 31 Dec 2023, Arrivo folded in 2018, and remaining efforts are short test tracks.
dismissed_by: Elon Musk's Alpha paper boosters and venture investors who funded Hyperloop One and peers
cost_of_error: Hundreds of millions in venture capital lost (Hyperloop One alone raised several hundred million) and years of public transit planning attention diverted from proven rail
lesson: A white paper from a famous founder is a hypothesis, not a cost estimate; when transport economists unanimously say the capacity and civil-works math does not close, the burden is on the builder to prove otherwise with a working segment.

quotes.text: there's no way the economics on that would ever work out.
quotes.speaker: Dan Sperling, director, Institute of Transportation Studies, UC Davis (as quoted on Wikipedia)

claim: Skeptics mocked the pre-launch hype: a $5,000, 10 mph scooter would not remake cities or replace the car.
what_happened: Segway planned up to 100,000 sales in 13 months but sold only ~140,000 in total; it survived as a niche for tours and security and the PT was discontinued in July 2020. Electric micro-mobility did arrive later, via cheap e-scooters (including from Segway-Ninebot).
dismissed_by: Dean Kamen, John Doerr (more important than the Internet) and Steve Jobs (as big a deal as the PC)
cost_of_error: Investors' heavy pre-launch funding never repaid; ~140,000 units lifetime vs 100,000 planned in first 13 months; company sold in 2009 and again to Ninebot in 2015
lesson: Skeptics can be right about the product and wrong about the category: the specific device flopped on price and form, while the underlying need was later met by a cheaper, simpler design.

thing: Mass adoption of private automobiles on city streets
claim: Cars were killing pedestrians, especially children and the elderly, at scale and should be speed-governed (Cincinnati's 1923 petition sought a 25 mph limiter on every car).
what_happened: The anti-car movement lost: auto dealers defeated the Cincinnati governor measure, the industry pushed the 1928 Model Municipal Traffic Ordinance and the crime of jaywalking, and streets were redefined for cars. The fear of mass death proved accurate, but the car still became the dominant mode and delivered huge mobility gains.
dismissed_by: Auto dealers, automakers, AAA and motor clubs, who reframed pedestrians as the problem through jaywalking campaigns
cost_of_error: Road deaths became a permanent toll of tens of thousands a year in the US (roughly 40,000 a year in the 2020s), disproportionately pedestrians
lesson: A technology can be both right about the harm and unstoppable; the fight that matters is who gets to write the rules about where the harm lands, and incumbents with sales at stake will write them if you do not.

quotes.text: Every car should be equipped with a device that would hold the speed down to whatever number of miles stipulated for the city in which its owner lived.
quotes.speaker: Illustrated World (1920), as quoted by Vox

thing: Fully autonomous consumer cars and robotaxis (Tesla FSD promised from 2016; industry-wide 2020 targets)
claim: Driverless cars will arrive far more slowly than promised, first as geofenced taxi services in restricted areas, not as cars that drive anywhere.
what_happened: Tesla sold FSD from 2016 and repeatedly promised full autonomy within a year or two; as of 2026 it remained supervised, with a small Austin robotaxi pilot from June 2025. Meanwhile Waymo did launch geofenced driverless taxi services, roughly on the skeptics' restricted-geography path, slightly earlier than Brooks' NET 2022 milestone.
dismissed_by: Elon Musk and Tesla, plus 2016-2018 industry forecasts of mass-market autonomy by ~2020
cost_of_error: Billions spent by consumers on FSD packages sold years before the capability; NHTSA investigations into Autopilot-involved crashes; Uber, Ford/Argo and GM Cruise wrote off or shut multibillion-dollar AV programs
lesson: Skeptics of a timeline are usually right about the date and wrong about never; bet on the constrained, geofenced version arriving and the everywhere version slipping.

quotes.text: Within some constraints, all these things will eventually be solved. But it is going to be much slower than many expect.
quotes.speaker: Rodney Brooks, MIT roboticist (dated predictions, 1 Jan 2018)

thing: Champlain Towers South, an aging 1981 reinforced-concrete beachfront condo with a defectively waterproofed pool deck
claim: The pool-deck waterproofing had failed and water was severely damaging the concrete slabs below; without prompt replacement the deterioration would expand exponentially.
what_happened: Repairs were delayed over cost and owner disputes; on 24 June 2021 the building partially collapsed at night, killing 98, and Florida passed mandatory milestone inspection and reserve laws in 2022.
dismissed_by: Surfside's chief building official, who told residents in 2018 the tower appeared in good shape, and a condo board that deferred the multimillion-dollar repair
cost_of_error: 98 deaths; $1.02bn victims' settlement (2022); condo insurance and special assessments across Florida rose several-fold
lesson: A written engineering warning that comes with a big bill tends to get deferred by committees that share the cost; the warning that predicts exponential deterioration is a deadline, not an estimate.

quotes.text: failure to replace waterproofing in the near future will cause the extent of the concrete deterioration to expand exponentially
quotes.speaker: Morabito Consultants, structural field survey report (Oct 2018), as quoted on Wikipedia

thing: Olympic-class liners (Titanic) carrying lifeboats sized to 1894 Board of Trade rules rather than to people aboard
claim: Harland & Wolff's Alexander Carlisle proposed davits and boats for up to 48 lifeboats; the 16 (plus 4 collapsibles) fitted under outdated rules could not hold everyone aboard.
what_happened: Titanic sank in April 1912 with lifeboat capacity for about 53% of those aboard; about 1,500 died and the 1914 SOLAS convention mandated lifeboat places for everyone.
dismissed_by: White Star Line and the Board of Trade, whose rules scaled lifeboats to tonnage not passengers, plus a shipbuilding belief that the ship itself was the lifeboat
cost_of_error: About 1,500 deaths; extra 32 boats would have cost some $16,000 against a $7.5m ship
lesson: Compliance with a rule written for a smaller generation of the technology is not safety; when the system outgrows the regulation, the gap is where the casualties come from.

quotes.text: I do not know why I did. I am not generally soft... But I must say I was very soft the day I signed that.
quotes.speaker: Alexander Carlisle, Harland & Wolff general manager (British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry testimony, as quoted on Wikipedia)
